CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral Contracepti:
What & Why

The COCP is a combined hormonal contraceptive containing both oestrogen (ethinylestradiol) and a progestogen. It’s one of the most widely used contraceptives, highly effective, with valuable non-contraceptive benefits (cycle control, acne, dysmenorrhoea) — but it carries oestrogen-related risks (VTE, arterial disease) that make safe prescribing via UKMEC and the missed-pill rules core examinable skills.

The whole topic hangs on three things: how it works, who can’t have it (UKMEC 3/4), and what to do when pills are missed.
Mechanism
  • Primary: inhibits ovulation — oestrogen + progestogen suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (↓FSH/LH) → no LH surge → no ovulation
  • Secondary: thickens cervical mucus (progestogen) + thins the endometrium
  • >99% effective with perfect use (~91% typical use); efficacy measured by the Pearl Index (pregnancies per 100 woman-years)
Starting & Taking the Pill
▶️ Starting
  • Within the first 5 days of the cycle → immediately effective, no extra cover
  • Any other time → 7 days of additional (barrier) contraception (exclude pregnancy first)
📅 Regimens
  • Traditional 21/7 — one pill daily for 21 days, then a 7-day pill-free interval (withdrawal bleed)
  • Tailored/extended (equally safe): tricycling (3 packs then a break) or continuous (no pill-free interval) — fewer withdrawal symptoms
  • Same time each day; sex in the break is only “safe” if the next pack starts on time
When is efficacy reduced? Vomiting within 2 h of a pill (take a replacement pill ASAP; missed-pill rules only if it recurs or persists >24h); drugs causing vomiting/diarrhoea (orlistat); liver enzyme-inducing drugs (rifampicin, some anticonvulsants, St John’s Wort) → use additional/alternative method.
The Decisive Skill — Missed Pills (the 48-hour rule)
📷 Image placeholder — Missed-pill decision flowchart — 1 vs 2+ pills, then the Week 1 (consider EC) / Week 2 (no EC) / Week 3 (omit pill-free interval) branch.
“Missed” = a pill taken >24 h late (i.e. >48 h since the last one). Verified against FSRH.
ScenarioAction
1 pill missed (anywhere)Take the missed pill ASAP (even if 2 in one day), continue as normal. No extra contraception needed.
2+ pills missedTake the most recent missed pill ASAP (discard earlier missed ones), continue pack, + condoms/abstain until 7 consecutive pills taken. Then apply the week rule ↓
For 2+ missed — the week determines emergency contraception need
📅 Week 1 (days 1–7)
  • Consider emergency contraception if unprotected sex occurred in the pill-free interval or week 1
📅 Week 2 (days 8–14)
  • No EC needed (provided the preceding 7 days were taken correctly)
📅 Week 3 (days 15–21)
  • Finish the current pack and start the next pack immediately — OMIT the pill-free interval
The logic: the danger of missed pills is extending the hormone-free interval (which lets ovulation escape). That’s why week 1 (adjacent to the break) is riskiest, and why in week 3 you skip the break to avoid a long gap.
UKMEC — Who Can/Can’t Have It
📷 Image placeholder — UKMEC 3 vs 4 at-a-glance — migraine with aura, age ≥35 & ≥15 cigs/day, VTE/thrombophilia, BP (140–159/90–99 = 3; ≥160/100 = 4), breastfeeding <6 wk, active breast cancer.
The UK Medical Eligibility Criteria grade suitability: 1 (no restriction) → 2 (benefits outweigh risks) → 3 (risks generally outweigh benefits — avoid unless no alternative) → 4 (unacceptable risk — do NOT use).
UKMEC 3 (relative — risks usually outweigh)
  • Age >35 and smoking <15/day
  • BMI >35
  • First-degree relative with VTE <45
  • Controlled hypertension
  • Immobility (e.g. wheelchair)
  • BRCA1/2 carrier
  • Current gallbladder disease
🚫 UKMEC 4 (absolute — unacceptable risk)
  • Migraine WITH AURA (any age — stroke risk; the classic answer)
  • Age >35 and smoking ≥15/day
  • History of VTE or thrombogenic mutation (Factor V Leiden)
  • History of stroke or ischaemic heart disease
  • Breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum
  • Uncontrolled hypertension
  • Current breast cancer
  • Major surgery with prolonged immobilisation
  • Positive antiphospholipid antibodies (e.g. in SLE)
Stop oestrogen-containing contraception 4 weeks before major/immobilising surgery (VTE risk). ALL hormonal contraception is contraindicated in active breast cancer — only barrier or copper IUD may be used.
Advantages & Disadvantages
✅ Advantages
  • Highly effective, reversible, doesn’t interfere with sex
  • Lighter, more regular, less painful periods (good for HMB, dysmenorrhoea, PMS)
  • Reduces ovarian, endometrial + colorectal cancer
  • Protects against PID; may reduce ovarian cysts, benign breast disease + acne
❌ Disadvantages
  • No STI protection; user-dependent (may forget)
  • Increased risk of VTE, breast cancer, cervical cancer, ischaemic heart disease, stroke
  • Temporary: headache, nausea, breast tenderness, mood changes, spotting
The elegant mnemonic: the COCP raises the risk of the cancers we screen for (breast, cervical) and protects against the ones we don’t (ovarian, endometrial).
Exam Pearls
What/mechanism
Oestrogen + progestogen; primary mechanism = inhibits ovulation. >99% effective (perfect use).
Starting
Start ≤day 5 → immediate cover; any other time → 7 days extra.
Missed pill
>48 h since last. 1 missed → take ASAP, no extra cover. 2+ missed → take ASAP + 7 days condoms + apply the week rule.
Week rule
Week 1 missed → consider EC; Week 2 → no EC; Week 3 → omit the pill-free interval (run packs together).
The danger
Lengthening the hormone-free interval.
UKMEC 4
Migraine WITH AURA, >35 & smoking ≥15/day, prior VTE/thrombophilia, stroke/IHD, uncontrolled HTN, current breast cancer, antiphospholipid antibodies, breastfeeding <6 wks.
Surgery / breast cancer
Stop 4 weeks before major surgery. Active breast cancer → only barrier/copper IUD.
Benefits
Lighter/regular periods; ↓ovarian, endometrial, colorectal cancer; protects against PID.
Mnemonic
Raises risk of screened cancers (breast/cervical), protects against unscreened (ovarian/endometrial).
CONTRACEPTION__Contraception in Special:
What & Why

Most contraceptive counselling follows standard UKMEC logic — but three groups need a modified approach because their physiology, risk profile, or goals differ: women over 40 (falling fertility, rising VTE/cardiovascular risk, when to stop), the postpartum woman (a thrombotic state, breastfeeding, rapid return of fertility), and trans/non-binary people (whose hormone therapy interacts with — but does not replace — contraception).

This is the reference card for those three groups; the method-specific rules live in their own notes.
Group 1 — Women Over 40
The core tension: fertility is declining but not gone (pregnancy is still possible and higher-risk here), while VTE, cardiovascular + cancer risks rise — so method choice shifts, and the new question is “when can she stop?”
Method-specific points (FSRH)
  • COCP: UKMEC 2 at ≥40 (no other risk factors) — usable up to age 50 in low-risk (non-smoking, no CVD risk) women. Perimenopausal benefits: maintains bone density + reduces vasomotor symptoms; a lower-dose (≤30 µg ethinylestradiol) pill is preferred
  • Depo-Provera (DMPA): small, usually reversible loss of BMD (bone mineral density) + a delay in return of fertility of up to 1 year → review regularly and weigh osteoporosis risk factors
  • LARC is ideal at this age (effective; the IUS treats coexisting HMB and can provide the progestogen arm of HRT)
When to stop contraception (FSRH)
  • All women can stop at age 55 — spontaneous conception is exceptionally rare beyond this, even with ongoing bleeding
  • Non-hormonal / barrier: stop after 1 year of amenorrhoea if ≥50, or 2 years if <50
  • Copper IUD inserted at ≥40 → can stay until the menopause (and 1 yr after LMP if ≥50 / 2 yrs if <50)
  • 52 mg LNG-IUS inserted at ≥45 → usable for contraception until 55
HRT is NOT contraceptive — a perimenopausal woman on HRT still needs contraception until the appropriate stopping point. A classic trap.
Group 2 — Postpartum Contraception
The core tension: the postpartum period is a prothrombotic state (oestrogen is dangerous early), fertility returns from ~day 21, and breastfeeding shapes what’s safe. (FSRH Contraception After Pregnancy.)
Contraception is needed from day 21 — before that the earliest ovulation risk is negligible.
🩸 Combined hormonal (COCP)
  • UKMEC 4 if breastfeeding <6 weeks; UKMEC 2 if 6 weeks–6 months
  • Avoid in ALL women in the first 21 days regardless of feeding — VTE risk (longer with additional risk factors — immobility, BMI ≥30, PPH, caesarean, pre-eclampsia, smoking → UKMEC 4 to 6 weeks)
  • After day 21 → 7 days extra cover; may reduce breast milk
💊 Progestogen-only + LARC
  • POP: start anytime; after day 21 → 2 days extra cover; only a small amount enters milk — harmless to the infant
  • Implant: anytime, safe in breastfeeding
  • IUD/IUS: insert within 48 h of birth OR after 4 weeks — not in between (perforation/expulsion risk); IUS contraindicated in breast cancer
Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM): up to 98% effective — but only if all three hold: fully breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + <6 months postpartum. Effectiveness falls once any criterion fails (supplementary feeds, periods return, or >6 months).
Group 3 — Trans & Non-Binary People
The core principle: gender-affirming hormone therapy is NOT contraception — pregnancy (or causing pregnancy) remains possible, so contraceptive need is assessed by anatomy and fertility, not gender identity.
🧑 Trans men / transmasculine (retained uterus + ovaries)
  • Avoid COCP / oestrogen-containing methods — oestrogen opposes testosterone therapy
  • Copper IUD — doesn’t interfere with hormone treatment
  • POP / implant / injection — progestogen-only methods don’t interfere with testosterone → suitable
  • Testosterone is teratogenic — effective contraception is essential; testosterone must NOT be relied on to prevent pregnancy
🧑 Trans women / transfeminine (assigned male at birth)
  • Feminising hormone therapy (oestrogen/anti-androgens) is NOT effective contraception
  • If a partner could become pregnant → advise condoms
General: use inclusive, sensitive language; assess individually; the same UKMEC framework applies to the retained reproductive anatomy.
Exam Pearls
Women >40 — method
COCP UKMEC 2 (usable to 50 if low-risk); helps bone density + menopausal symptoms; Depo → BMD loss + up to 1-yr fertility delay.
Women >40 — stopping
Stop all contraception at 55. Non-hormonal: 1 yr amenorrhoea if ≥50, 2 yrs if <50. HRT is NOT contraception.
Postpartum — timing
Contraception from day 21. COCP UKMEC 4 if breastfeeding <6 wks; avoid in ALL women first 21 days (VTE).
Postpartum — methods
POP/implant anytime; IUD/IUS within 48 h or after 4 wks (not between).
LAM
98% only if: fully breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + <6 months (all three).
Trans
Gender-affirming hormones ≠ contraception.
Trans men
Can conceive → avoid COCP (oestrogen opposes testosterone); use copper IUD or progestogen-only; testosterone is teratogenic.
Trans women
Hormones aren’t contraceptive → condoms.
CONTRACEPTION__Contraception — Overview:
What & Why

Contraception is the prevention of pregnancy, and this overview is the map of the whole system — the framework that lets you counsel a woman toward the right method for her. Contraceptive choice is rarely about “the best method” in the abstract — it’s about matching a method to the individual (her preferences, medical eligibility via UKMEC, whether she wants something she doesn’t have to think about, and her wider circumstances).

The examinable skill: know the categories of method, how effectiveness is measured, the cross-cutting rules, and how to structure a counselling conversation.
Measuring Effectiveness — the Pearl Index
📷 Image placeholder — Typical vs perfect use — COCP ~9% vs ~0.3% failure/year; implant/IUS <0.1% (typical ≈ perfect) — the core reason LARC is 'most effective'.
  • Pearl Index = pregnancies per 100 woman-years of use. A Pearl Index of 0.2 = 0.2 pregnancies per 100 women per year (2 per 1000)
  • Lower = more effective
  • Distinguish perfect use (correct + consistent) from typical use (real-world, including errors) — the gap is large for user-dependent methods (pills) and negligible for LARC
The Organising Fork — LARC vs User-Dependent
📷 Image placeholder — Enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. rifampicin, certain antiepileptics) reduce efficacy of the implant, POP, COCP and patch — but NOT the injectable, IUD or IUS.

The most useful way to carve up the methods is by whether they depend on the user remembering something — this drives real-world effectiveness and the “LARC-first” counselling emphasis.

🎯 LARC — “fit and forget” (most effective; typical ≈ perfect use)
  • Progestogen implant (Nexplanon) — the single most effective method
  • IUS (levonorgestrel) + copper IUD
  • Injectable (Depo-Provera / DMPA)
⏱️ Short-acting hormonal (user-dependent)
  • Combined (oestrogen + progestogen): COCP, combined patch (Evra), vaginal ring
  • Progestogen-only: POP
🛡️ Barrier / natural
  • Male/female condoms — the only methods that protect against STIs; diaphragm/cap
  • Fertility awareness / cycle tracking; lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM)
🚨 Emergency + permanent
  • Emergency: levonorgestrel, ulipristal acetate, copper IUD (the most effective EC)
  • Permanent: female sterilisation (tubal occlusion), vasectomy
How the Hormonal Methods Work
MethodMechanism
Combined (oestrogen + progestogen)Primarily inhibit ovulation (suppress FSH/LH) + thicken cervical mucus + thin endometrium
Progestogen-onlyMainly thicken cervical mucus + thin endometrium; ovulation inhibition varies — reliable with desogestrel POP, implant + injectable, but NOT the traditional POP
Copper IUDCopper is toxic to sperm + ova (and impairs implantation) — non-hormonal
LNG-IUSLocal progestogen → thins endometrium, thickens mucus
Cross-Cutting Rule — Breast Cancer
ALL hormonal contraception is contraindicated in active breast cancer. Only barrier methods or the copper IUD may be used.
The Combined Patch (Evra)
  • The only combined patch licensed in the UK. Worn + changed weekly for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week (withdrawal bleed)
  • Delayed change ≤48 h (weeks 1–2): change immediately, no extra cover
  • >48 h: change + 7 days barrier + consider EC if UPSI in the last 5 days or during an extended patch-free interval
  • Week 3 delay: remove + restart on the usual cycle-start day; no extra cover. Patch-free-week delay: 7 days extra cover at the start of the new cycle
The Evra rules mirror the COCP 48-hour logic — the danger is again lengthening the hormone-free interval.
Structuring the Counselling Conversation
  • 1. Explore needs & preferences — reversibility, future fertility, something non-daily (LARC), STI protection, or non-contraceptive benefits (acne, HMB, cycle control)?
  • 2. Assess medical eligibility (UKMEC) — focused history: VTE/thrombophilia, migraine with aura, smoking + age >35, breast cancer, BP/BMI, breastfeeding, liver disease, enzyme-inducing drugs
  • 3. Explain the options — effectiveness (typical vs perfect use), how it’s used, side effects, risks/benefits, STI protection (barrier only)
  • 4. Support informed choice — highlight that LARC methods are the most effective; use decision aids
  • 5. Safety-net — missed-method rules, when to seek emergency contraception, follow-up (BP/eligibility review for CHC, annual review)
  • 6. Confidentiality & young people — for under-16s, apply Fraser guidelines (competence to consent to contraceptive advice/treatment)
Special groups get their own approach — women over 40, the postpartum period, and trans/non-binary people each modify the standard logic (see the dedicated Contraception in Special Groups note).
Exam Pearls
Pearl Index
Pregnancies per 100 woman-years; lower = better. Distinguish typical vs perfect use (huge for pills, negligible for LARC).
LARC
Implant, IUS, IUD, injection = most effective (not user-dependent). Implant is the single most effective.
STIs
Only barrier methods protect against STIs.
Mechanisms
Combined → inhibit ovulation; progestogen-only → mainly mucus/endometrium (ovulation inhibition reliable only with desogestrel POP/implant/injectable); copper IUD → toxic to sperm/ova (non-hormonal).
Breast cancer
Active breast cancer → NO hormonal contraception; only barrier or copper IUD.
Evra patch
Weekly ×3 then patch-free week; 48-hour rule as for COCP.
Counselling
Preferences → UKMEC eligibility → explain options → informed choice → safety-net; Fraser guidelines for under-16s.
Emergency
Copper IUD is the most effective EC.
CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive Implant:
What & Why

The contraceptive implant is a small progestogen-only rod inserted under the skin of the upper arm giving 3 years of highly effective contraception. It’s the single most effective contraceptive method available (more effective than sterilisation), a LARC (“fit and forget” → real-world effectiveness matches perfect use), and oestrogen-free — usable when the COCP is contraindicated (VTE history, migraine with aura).

The device: Nexplanon — a single rod containing 68 mg etonogestrel (a progestogen), released slowly over 3 years. It’s radiopaque (contains barium sulphate) so it can be located on X-ray/imaging if impalpable — the key advantage over the older Implanon.
Mechanism of Action
Primary mechanism = inhibition of ovulation — etonogestrel suppresses the LH surge → no ovulation (reaching ovulation-inhibiting levels within ~1 day of insertion). Correction: the primary MOA is ovulation inhibition, not mucus thickening (per FSRH/manufacturer).
  • Primary: inhibits ovulation (LH-surge suppression)
  • Secondary: thickens cervical mucus (barrier to sperm) + thins the endometrium
Insertion & Timing
📷 Image placeholder — Insertion site — subdermal, medial aspect of the non-dominant upper arm overlying the triceps, ~8–10 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle.
  • Inserted subdermally in the proximal, non-dominant upper arm, overlying the triceps (medial aspect), by a trained professional
  • Days 1–5 of the cycle → immediately effective, no extra cover. Any other time → 7 days additional contraception (and exclude pregnancy)
  • Can be inserted immediately following an abortion or miscarriage (or postpartum)
  • Lasts 3 years, then removed/replaced; rapid return of fertility after removal (etonogestrel clears within ~a week)
Advantages & Disadvantages
✅ Advantages
  • The most effective method (failure <0.1 per 100 women over 3 years; not user-dependent)
  • Long-acting (3 years)
  • Oestrogen-free → usable with VTE history, migraine with aura, other oestrogen contraindications
  • Rapidly reversible; immediate post-abortion/miscarriage/postpartum insertion; may reduce dysmenorrhoea
❌ Disadvantages
  • Requires a trained professional to insert + remove
  • No STI protection
  • 7 days extra cover if not inserted on days 1–5
  • Irregular bleeding (the main drawback)
  • Rare: implant migration, neurovascular injury at insertion, difficult removal if placed too deep
Adverse Effects
Irregular/unpredictable bleeding is the main issue + the commonest reason for discontinuation — from amenorrhoea (welcome) to frequent/prolonged bleeding. About half achieve amenorrhoea or an acceptable pattern; the first 6 months don’t reliably predict the later pattern.
🩸 Managing problematic bleeding
  • First exclude other causes — speculum exam + STI (chlamydia) check; consider cervical pathology if it persists
  • Trial of co-prescribed COCP (1–3 months) can settle it (or mefenamic acid / tranexamic acid / a progestogen)
💊 Other effects
  • Progestogenic: headache, nausea, breast pain/tenderness, mood changes, acne
  • No significant effect on BMD (bone mineral density) — unlike the injectable (a useful contrast)
Interactions & Contraindications (UKMEC)
📷 Image placeholder — UKMEC at a glance — 4 = current breast cancer; 3 = past breast cancer, IHD/stroke arising on method, unexplained vaginal bleeding pre-evaluation, severe cirrhosis/liver cancer.
Enzyme-inducing drugs reduce efficacy — rifampicin, some anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin), St John’s Wort. The implant relies on maintaining etonogestrel levels → use additional/alternative contraception (a copper IUD is often preferred).
🚫 UKMEC 4 (do not use)
  • Current breast cancer
UKMEC 3 (relative — usually avoid)
  • Ischaemic heart disease/stroke developing on the method
  • Unexplained/suspicious vaginal bleeding (before evaluation)
  • Past breast cancer
  • Severe (decompensated) liver cirrhosis, liver cancer
Otherwise UKMEC 1–2 for most conditions — its oestrogen-free profile makes it broadly usable.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Nexplanon = single etonogestrel rod, 3 years, subdermal in the non-dominant upper arm; radiopaque (locatable on X-ray).
MOA
Primary = inhibits ovulation (mucus/endometrium secondary).
Effectiveness
The single MOST effective contraceptive (LARC, not user-dependent).
Oestrogen-free
Usable with VTE history / migraine with aura.
Timing
Insert days 1–5 → immediate; otherwise 7 days extra cover. Immediate post-abortion insertion OK.
Main problem
Irregular bleeding = commonest reason to stop → exclude STI/pathology (speculum + chlamydia), then trial COCP.
Interactions
Enzyme inducers reduce efficacy → additional/alternative method (copper IUD).
UKMEC
4 = current breast cancer; 3 = past breast cancer, IHD/stroke on method, suspicious bleeding, severe liver disease.
Bone
No significant effect on BMD (contrast with Depo).
CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive Injection (:
What & Why

The contraceptive injection is a long-acting progestogen given by injection every ~12 weeks. It’s a LARC (effective, not dependent on daily adherence), oestrogen-free (usable where oestrogen is contraindicated), and carries three examinable, distinctive drawbacks that separate it from the other progestogen methods: an irreversible ~3-month duration, delayed return of fertility (up to a year), and an effect on bone mineral density.

The main agent: Depo-Provera — containing medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) 150 mg, given by deep IM injection every 12 weeks. Sayana Press is a subcutaneous DMPA (104 mg), bioequivalent + self-administered (useful in obesity or bleeding disorders/anticoagulation).
A 14-week window: it can be given up to 14 weeks after the last dose without needing extra precautions (i.e. up to 2 weeks late is fine).
Mechanism of Action
  • Primary: inhibits ovulation (suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary axis → no LH surge)
  • Secondary: thickens cervical mucus + thins the endometrium
The contrast: for Depo the primary MOA is ovulation inhibition — and unlike the traditional POP, this is reliable, which is why it’s so effective.
Administration & Timing
📷 Image placeholder — Injection-timing timeline — on-time/late (≤14 weeks: just re-inject, no extra cover) vs overdue (>14 weeks: exclude pregnancy + 7 days extra cover ± EC).
  • Deep IM injection every 12 weeks — gluteal (preferred, especially if obese), deltoid, or lateral thigh. Sayana Press is SC (abdomen/thigh)
  • Days 1–5 of the cycle → immediately effective; any other time → 7 days additional contraception (and exclude pregnancy)
  • ≤14 weeks since last dose → just give the next injection, no extra cover. >14 weeks (overdue) → exclude pregnancy, use extra cover for 7 days
Advantages & Disadvantages
✅ Advantages
  • Highly effective LARC (perfect-use failure ~0.2%), not user-dependent between injections
  • Oestrogen-free → usable with VTE history, migraine with aura
  • Only needed every 12 weeks; private (nothing to store/carry)
  • Reduces menstrual pain; often causes amenorrhoea; may help HMB + endometriosis; reduces PID / ovarian + endometrial cancer risk
❌ Disadvantages
  • Cannot be reversed once given — effects last ~3 months, so side effects persist until it wears off
  • Delayed return of fertility — up to ~12 months (median to conception ~9–10 months)
  • No STI protection
  • Not suitable if injections can’t be attended reliably
Adverse Effects
📷 Image placeholder — BMD-and-age at a glance — reversible bone loss; UKMEC 2 under-18 and over-45; review continued use from 45 and switch by ~50.
  • Irregular bleeding — common early; many progress to amenorrhoea with continued use
  • Weight gain — recognised (~2–3 kg over the first year; the method most clearly associated with weight gain)
  • Progestogenic effects: headache, mood changes/depression, breast tenderness, reduced libido, acne
Reduced BMD (bone mineral density) → potential ↑ osteoporosis risk — DMPA lowers oestrogen, reducing BMD; loss is greatest in the first 1–2 years then plateaus, and is largely recovered after stopping.
Age caveats: because of the BMD effect, DMPA is UKMEC 2 in adolescents (<18) (used when other methods unsuitable) and warrants review of benefits/risks from age 45 (UKMEC 2 for age >45) (encourage an alternative by ~50) and those with osteoporosis risk factors. WHO/FSRH place no restriction on duration for women 18–45 otherwise eligible.
Contraindications (UKMEC)
🚫 UKMEC 4 (do not use)
  • Current breast cancer
UKMEC 3 (relative — usually avoid)
  • Past breast cancer
  • Multiple cardiovascular risk factors; current IHD/stroke
  • Distinctively for DMPA — significant risk factors for osteoporosis (given the BMD effect)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Depo-Provera = DMPA 150 mg, deep IM every 12 weeks (Sayana Press = SC 104 mg, self-administered).
14-week window
Can be given up to 2 weeks late without extra cover.
MOA
Primary = inhibits ovulation (reliable — unlike traditional POP). Oestrogen-free LARC; often causes amenorrhoea.
Three signature drawbacks
(1) irreversible for ~3 months once given; (2) delayed return of fertility up to ~1 year; (3) reduced BMD.
Weight gain
The classic side effect (more than other methods).
Bone
BMD loss largely reversible; UKMEC 2 in under-18s and over-45s; review from 45 / osteoporosis risk.
UKMEC
4 = current breast cancer; 3 = past breast cancer + osteoporosis risk factors. No STI protection.
CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive Patch:
What & Why

The combined contraceptive patch is a combined hormonal contraceptive (oestrogen + progestogen) delivered transdermally — a small adhesive patch changed weekly. It’s a combined method for women who want the COCP’s benefits but not a daily pill — the same efficacy, contraindications and risk profile, but with a weekly action that suits adherence.

The examinable essence: it behaves like the COCP (same UKMEC, same oestrogen risks) but has its own “delayed change” rules, which parallel the COCP’s 48-hour logic.
The device: Evra — the only combined patch licensed in the UK — releasing ethinylestradiol + norelgestromin transdermally (bypassing first-pass metabolism → steady hormone levels).
Mechanism
  • Primary: inhibits ovulation (oestrogen + progestogen suppress FSH/LH)
  • Secondary: thickens cervical mucus, thins the endometrium
  • >99% effective with perfect use (~91% typical use) — same as the COCP
The Regimen
  • Weeks 1–3: wear a patch, changed every week (a new patch each week, same “change day”)
  • Week 4: patch-free week → a withdrawal bleed, then start the next cycle
  • Like the COCP, can be used in tailored/extended regimens (no patch-free week, or tricycling)
  • Starting: days 1–5 of the cycle → immediately effective; any other time → 7 days extra cover
The Decisive Skill — Delayed Patch Change
📷 Image placeholder — One-glance algorithm by patch week — Week 1/2 lapse (<48h vs >48h), Week 3 over-run, and late new-cycle start — mapped to extra-cover/EC actions.
The logic mirrors the COCP: the danger is extending the hormone-free interval, so timing relative to the patch-free week matters.
① End of Week 1 or 2 (mid-cycle patch)
  • Delay <48 h: apply a new patch immediately → no extra precautions
  • Delay >48 h: apply a new patch, start a new 4-week cycle (this becomes the new day 1/change day), + barrier for 7 days
  • Consider EC if unprotected sex in the preceding 5 days or during an extended patch-free interval
② End of Week 3 (over-run)
  • Remove the patch ASAP and apply the next patch on the usual cycle start day — even if a withdrawal bleed is occurring
  • No additional contraception needed
③ Delayed application after the patch-free week (new cycle's first patch late)
  • Any delay at the start of a new patch cycle extends the hormone-free interval → additional contraception for 7 days
  • Consider EC if unprotected sex during the extended patch-free interval
The unifying rule: a >48-hour lapse (or a delayed start to a new cycle) means the patch may not be working → 7 days extra cover ± EC. A short (<48 h) mid-cycle lapse is covered.
Detachment
  • <48 h: reapply (or apply a new patch) immediately; no extra cover; keep the same change day
  • ≥48 h (or unknown): start a new cycle as above + 7 days extra cover ± EC
  • If it won’t re-stick, apply a new patch (don’t use tape)
Advantages & Disadvantages
📷 Image placeholder — Higher total oestrogen exposure than a comparable COCP (~60% greater AUC despite lower peak) — VTE/arterial risk is at least as high as the pill, not lower.
✅ Advantages
  • Weekly, not daily → easier adherence for some
  • Same non-contraceptive benefits as COCP (lighter/regular periods, cycle control)
  • Unaffected by vomiting/diarrhoea (transdermal — an advantage over the COCP)
❌ Disadvantages
  • Same oestrogen risks as COCP (VTE, arterial disease) + same UKMEC contraindications — migraine with aura, VTE history, >35 & smoking ≥15/day → UKMEC 4 (<15/day = UKMEC 3)
  • Visible; can cause skin irritation at the site
  • Reduced efficacy if ≥90 kg — consider an alternative
  • No STI protection
Exam Pearls
What it is
Evra = the only combined patch in the UK; ethinylestradiol + norelgestromin, transdermal.
Regimen
Patch changed weekly for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week (withdrawal bleed).
Same as COCP
Same efficacy, UKMEC contraindications + oestrogen risks (migraine with aura, VTE, >35 + smoking ≥15/day = UKMEC 4).
Delayed change
<48 h mid-cycle → new patch, no extra cover. >48 h → new cycle + 7 days cover ± EC.
Week 3 / new cycle
Week 3 over-run → remove, restart on usual day, no extra cover. Late start of new cycle → 7 days cover.
Weight caveat
Reduced efficacy if ≥90 kg.
Advantage / caveat
Advantage over COCP: unaffected by vomiting/diarrhoea. No STI protection; skin irritation possible.
CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Contraception:
What & Why

Emergency contraception (EC) is used after unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI) or contraceptive failure to prevent pregnancy. It’s time-critical (efficacy falls with delay), the three methods differ sharply in mechanism, window and effectiveness, and the copper IUD — the most effective option — is consistently under-offered.

The core principle: oral EC works mainly by delaying/inhibiting ovulation — so it’s ineffective once ovulation has already occurred, and useless if already pregnant. The copper IUD is different: it works after fertilisation too (blocks implantation), so it’s the most effective and works at any point in the cycle.
The Decisive Fork — Which Method?
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side comparison of copper IUD vs ulipristal vs levonorgestrel — brand, window, mechanism and relative effectiveness at a glance.
Copper IUDUlipristal (UPA)Levonorgestrel (LNG)
Brand—EllaOneLevonelle
TypeCopper coilSelective progesterone receptor modulatorProgestogen
WindowUp to 5 days after UPSI (or 5 days after earliest likely ovulation)Up to 120 h (5 days)Up to 72 h (3 days)
MechanismToxic to sperm/ova + blocks implantationInhibits/delays ovulationInhibits/delays ovulation
EffectivenessMost effective (~99%), any time in cycleMore effective than LNG (works closer to ovulation)Least effective; falls with time
The rule: offer the copper IUD first (most effective, unaffected by weight or enzyme inducers) — then oral EC if declined or unsuitable. (In practice most women choose oral EC.)
1. Copper IUD — the Most Effective EC
📷 Image placeholder — Cycle timeline showing the two insertion windows — within 5 days of UPSI OR up to 5 days after earliest likely ovulation (~day 19 of a 28-day cycle).
  • The most effective emergency contraceptive (~99%) — offer to all women who meet the criteria
  • Effective regardless of where she is in the cycle (works post-fertilisation)
  • Timing: insert within 5 days of UPSI; OR, if later, up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation (≈ day 19 of a 28-day cycle)
  • Unaffected by weight/BMI or enzyme-inducing drugs — a key advantage
  • Consider prophylactic antibiotics if high STI risk at insertion
  • Can be left in situ for ongoing long-term contraception — a major bonus. If she wants it removed, keep it in until her next period
2. Ulipristal Acetate (UPA — EllaOne)
  • A selective progesterone receptor modulator → delays ovulation (effective even close to ovulation, when LNG is failing)
  • Single 30 mg oral dose, ASAP, no later than 120 hours (5 days) after UPSI
  • Can be used more than once in a cycle (but not with LNG in the same episode)
  • Reduced efficacy if BMI >30 — less weight-sensitive than LNG but not immune
Interaction rules (high-yield): UPA and progestogens interfere with each other. Progestogen in the 7 days before UPA can reduce its efficacy. Wait 5 days after UPA before starting/restarting hormonal contraception (use barrier methods meanwhile). Don’t use UPA + levonorgestrel together in the same episode.
Caution/avoid in severe asthma controlled by oral steroids (anti-progesterone effect). Breastfeeding: LNG is preferred (no restriction); after a single UPA dose, advise expressing & discarding breast milk for 1 week (limited infant-safety data).
3. Levonorgestrel (LNG — Levonelle)
  • Progestogen → inhibits/delays ovulation. The established mechanism is ovulation delay — a post-implantation effect is not established, and it does NOT disrupt an existing pregnancy
  • Single 1.5 mg oral dose, ASAP, within 72 hours (3 days) of UPSI — efficacy falls with time
  • Double the dose to 3 mg if BMI >26 or weight >70 kg (higher body weight lowers serum levels → reduced efficacy)
  • Also double to 3 mg if on enzyme-inducing drugs (or within the last 4 weeks) — though a copper IUD is preferred here
  • Repeat the dose if vomiting occurs within 3 hours
  • Can be used more than once in a cycle; hormonal contraception can start immediately after LNG (unlike UPA); no restrictions in breastfeeding
Practical Points Across All Methods
  • Take/insert ASAP — efficacy falls with delay for the oral methods
  • “Quick starting”: after LNG → start regular hormonal contraception immediately (+ 7 days barrier depending on method); after UPA → wait 5 days, use barrier meanwhile
  • Pregnancy test if the next period is >5–7 days late or lighter than usual
  • STI risk assessment + safeguarding (under-16 → Fraser guidelines)
  • EC is ineffective if ovulation has already happened (or if already pregnant) — the copper IUD is the fallback as it also blocks implantation
Exam Pearls
Three methods
Copper IUD (5 days, ~99%, MOST effective), ulipristal/EllaOne (120 h), levonorgestrel/Levonelle (72 h).
Copper IUD
First-line by effectiveness — offer to all; works any time in cycle; unaffected by weight/enzyme inducers; can stay for ongoing contraception. Timing: within 5 days of UPSI OR 5 days after earliest likely ovulation.
LNG
1.5 mg within 72 h; DOUBLE to 3 mg if BMI >26 / weight >70 kg, or on enzyme inducers; repeat if vomiting <3 h.
UPA
30 mg within 120 h; more effective than LNG (works near ovulation); caution in severe asthma on oral steroids.
Quick-start
After UPA, wait 5 DAYS before starting hormonal contraception (barrier meanwhile); after LNG, start immediately. Don’t combine UPA + LNG.
Mechanism
Oral EC works by delaying ovulation → ineffective once ovulation has occurred. Both oral methods usable more than once per cycle.
Breastfeeding
LNG — no restriction; UPA — express & discard milk for 1 week.
CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine Device & Sys:
What & Why

Intrauterine contraception is a small T-shaped device placed inside the uterus for long-acting, highly effective, reversible contraception (LARC). Two types with fundamentally different mechanisms: the copper IUD (non-hormonal) and the levonorgestrel IUS (hormonal, e.g. Mirena). Both are >99% effective, “fit and forget”, and among the most cost-effective methods.

The choice turns on the effect on periods: the copper coil makes bleeding worse; the hormonal IUS makes it better and treats HMB.
The Decisive Fork — Copper IUD vs Levonorgestrel IUS
📷 Image placeholder — Lower-dose LNG-IUS options — Kyleena (19.5 mg, 5y) and Jaydess (13.5 mg, 3y) are smaller with more bleeding and no HMB/HRT indication; only the 52 mg IUS (Mirena) is licensed for HMB and endometrial protection.
Copper IUD (“the coil”)Levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena)
TypeNon-hormonal (copper)Hormonal (progestogen)
MechanismCopper toxic to sperm (↓motility & survival) + impairs implantationLevonorgestrel → thins endometrium + thickens cervical mucus
Effect on periodsHeavier, longer, more painfulLighter → often amenorrhoea; treats HMB
HMB / menorrhagiaNot recommended (worsens it)First-line treatment
Effective fromImmediatelyAfter 7 days (immediate if inserted days 1–5)
Duration5 or 10 years (device-dependent)Now 8 years for 52 mg (Mirena) — updated
Emergency contraceptionYes — the most effective ECNo
The clean rule: the IUS is particularly useful with coexisting problems — HMB/menorrhagia, or where you’d avoid oestrogen (hypertension). The copper IUD is best avoided in menorrhagia (worsens it) but is ideal if she wants a hormone-free method.
Mechanism of Action
🔩 Copper IUD (non-hormonal)
  • Copper ions are toxic to sperm (↓motility + survival) and ova → prevents fertilisation
  • Produces an endometrial inflammatory reaction that impairs implantation
💊 Levonorgestrel IUS
  • Local progestogen → prevents endometrial proliferation (thin endometrium) + thickens cervical mucus
  • Ovulation usually not suppressed (acts locally)
Effectiveness & Duration
  • Both >99% effective (failure ~0.2–0.8% year 1) — not user-dependent, and unaffected by weight/BMI or enzyme-inducing drugs (a big advantage over pills/implant)
  • Copper IUD: copper on the stem only → 5 years; copper on the stem and arms → up to 10 years
  • IUS (Mirena, 52 mg LNG, ~20 µg/24h): now licensed for 8 years for contraception (updated from 5 — FSRH/licence extension, Jan 2024)
  • As endometrial protection with oestrogen-only HRT, licensed for 5 years — the HMB/HRT durations were NOT extended
  • If inserted at age ≥45, can be used for contraception until age 55
Counselling & Timing
📷 Image placeholder — Copper IUD as emergency contraception — effective up to 5 days after UPSI, or up to 5 days after the earliest estimated ovulation; the most effective EC and provides ongoing contraception.
  • Copper IUD → reliable immediately after insertion (useful as EC)
  • IUS → reliable after 7 days (extra cover for 7 days) — unless inserted in the first 5 days of the cycle (then immediate)
  • Teach the woman to feel for the threads after each period (check it’s in place)
  • Rapid return of fertility on removal
Potential Issues / Complications
🩸 Altered bleeding
  • Copper IUD: periods heavier, longer, more painful
  • IUS: irregular bleeding/spotting first ~3–6 months, then light/infrequent — often amenorrhoea, less dysmenorrhoea
Insertion-related risks
  • PID risk — small increase, confined to the first ~20 days (screen for STIs first); baseline thereafter
  • Perforation — rare (~1–2/1000; higher if fixed/retroverted uterus or early postpartum)
  • Expulsion — ~1 in 20, highest in the first few months
If pregnancy occurs with an IUD/IUS in situ → a higher proportion are ectopic (though the absolute ectopic risk is lower than using no contraception, as overall pregnancy is rare) → exclude ectopic if pregnant. “Lost threads” → could mean expulsion, perforation or pregnancy → exclude pregnancy, locate device (USS).
Contraindications
  • Current pelvic inflammatory disease / current STI / puerperal or post-abortal sepsis — defer until treated
  • Unexplained vaginal bleeding (before evaluation); uterine cavity distortion (fibroids/anomalies)
  • Current breast cancer — the IUS specifically (hormonal)
  • Wilson’s disease / copper allergy — specific to the copper IUD
  • Cervical/endometrial cancer, current trophoblastic disease
Exam Pearls
Two types
Copper IUD (non-hormonal) vs LNG-IUS/Mirena (hormonal). Both >99%, LARC, unaffected by weight/enzyme inducers.
Copper IUD
MOA = copper toxic to sperm/ova (+ blocks implantation); makes periods HEAVIER → avoid in menorrhagia; but is the MOST effective EC and reliable immediately.
IUS
MOA = thins endometrium + thickens mucus; makes periods LIGHTER → 1st-line for HMB; reliable after 7 days.
Durations
Copper 5 or 10 years; Mirena now 8 years (updated from 5); IUS-for-HRT 5 years.
PID
Risk only in the first ~20 days after insertion (screen for STIs first).
Perforation / expulsion
Perforation ~1–2/1000; expulsion ~1 in 20 (highest early).
Ectopic
Pregnancy with a coil in situ → higher proportion ectopic → exclude ectopic. Teach thread-checking; lost threads → exclude expulsion/perforation/pregnancy.
CI
Current PID/STI, unexplained bleeding, cavity distortion; copper — Wilson’s; IUS — current breast cancer.
CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-Only Pill (PO:
What & Why

The POP (“mini-pill”) is a daily oral contraceptive containing only a progestogen — no oestrogen. It’s the go-to oral method when oestrogen is contraindicated (the situations that make the COCP UKMEC 3/4 — VTE history, migraine with aura, >35 & smoking, breastfeeding) — with very few contraindications, usable by almost anyone.

The examinable essence: its strict daily timing — the missed-pill window is much tighter than the COCP and differs by pill type (3 hours traditional, 12 hours desogestrel), the single most tested POP fact.
The core contrast with the COCP: no oestrogen → no oestrogen-related risks (VTE, arterial disease) → far broader eligibility, but at the cost of less forgiving timing and less predictable bleeding.
Mechanism of Action
📷 Image placeholder — Traditional POP (mucus-thickening, ovulation inhibited in only ~50–60% of cycles) vs desogestrel/drospirenone (reliable ovulation inhibition → longer window).
💊 Traditional POPs (levonorgestrel, norethisterone)
  • Work mainly by thickening cervical mucus (barrier to sperm) + endometrial thinning + reduced tubal motility
  • Inhibit ovulation in only ~50–60% of cycles → the mucus effect is the mainstay
  • The mucus effect is short-lived → hence the strict 3-hour window
⚡ Desogestrel POP (+ newer drospirenone POP)
  • Also reliably inhibit ovulation (in addition to the mucus effect)
  • This is why they’re more effective and allow a longer missed-pill window (the desogestrel POP’s anovulatory action is the reason for its 12-hour window)
The Decisive Skill — Missed-Pill Window (by pill type)
📷 Image placeholder — Missed-pill window comparison — traditional POP >3h, desogestrel (Cerazette) >12h, drospirenone (Slynd) >24h, all needing condoms until 48h of correct pill-taking.
POP typeMissed if taken...Extra cover after a missed pill
Traditional POP (levonorgestrel, norethisterone)>3 hours lateCondoms until 48 h of correct pill-taking re-established
Desogestrel POP (Cerazette)>12 hours lateCondoms until 48 h re-established
Drospirenone POP (Slynd — newer)>24 hours lateHas a 4-day hormone-free interval; different rules
Action if a pill is missed: take the missed pill ASAP (even if 2 in one day); take the next at the usual time. If >1 missed → just take one (the most recent), continue the pack. Use condoms until pills taken correctly for 48 hours (~48 h to re-thicken cervical mucus). Consider EC if unprotected sex occurred during the unprotected window. Vomiting within 2 h (or severe diarrhoea) → treat as a missed pill.
Starting the POP
  • Started up to and including day 5 of the cycle → immediate protection
  • Any other time → 48 hours (2 days) of additional contraception (~48 h for cervical mucus to thicken)
  • Switching from the COCP: immediate protection if continued directly from the end of an active pill packet (straight after day 21, no gap)
  • Taken at the same time every day, continuously — NO pill-free break (unlike the COCP)
Interactions
Ordinary antibiotics: no extra precautions needed — non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics do NOT reduce efficacy (a common misconception).
EXCEPT enzyme-inducing drugs — rifampicin/rifabutin and other P450 inducers (some anticonvulsants, St John’s Wort) reduce efficacy → use additional/alternative contraception (a non-hormonal method is preferred).
Adverse Effects
  • Irregular vaginal bleeding — the most common problem (unpredictable spotting/bleeding, or amenorrhoea; the leading reason for discontinuation). If persistent >3 months, exclude other causes (STI, pregnancy, cervical pathology)
  • Breast tenderness, weight gain (perceived), acne, headache, mood changes
  • Small increased risk of ovarian cysts
  • Ectopic pregnancy: the traditional POP (doesn’t always stop ovulation) carries a slightly higher proportion of ectopics if pregnancy occurs → exclude ectopic if a POP user becomes pregnant with pain (overall, any contraception lowers absolute ectopic risk vs none)
Contraindications (few — the POP’s key advantage)
🚫 UKMEC 4 (do not use)
  • Current breast cancer — the main absolute contraindication
UKMEC 3 (relative)
  • Past breast cancer
  • Active/severe liver disease/cirrhosis or liver tumours
  • (Developing on the method) stroke/IHD
  • Unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation (UKMEC 2 for the POP)
Otherwise usable in almost everyone — including where the COCP is contraindicated (VTE history, migraine with aura, >35 & smoking, hypertension, breastfeeding) — its key selling point.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Progestogen only, no oestrogen → usable where COCP is contraindicated (VTE, migraine with aura, >35+smoking, breastfeeding).
MOA
Traditional POP = thickens cervical mucus (ovulation inhibited in only ~50–60%). Desogestrel/drospirenone also inhibit ovulation → longer window.
Missed-pill window
3 hours (traditional) / 12 hours (desogestrel/Cerazette) / 24 hours (drospirenone/Slynd).
Missed pill
Take ASAP + condoms until 48 h of correct pills (± EC if UPSI).
Starting
Start ≤day 5 → immediate; otherwise 48 h extra cover. Taken continuously, no pill-free break.
Antibiotics
Ordinary antibiotics DON’T reduce efficacy — only enzyme inducers (rifampicin) do.
Side effects
Irregular bleeding = commonest side effect / reason to stop.
UKMEC / ectopic
UKMEC 4 = current breast cancer (few other CIs). Traditional POP → slightly higher proportion ectopic if pregnancy occurs → exclude ectopic.
CONTRACEPTION__Contraception in Special:
What & Why

Contraception in special groups means tailoring contraceptive choice to circumstances that change eligibility, safety, or the practicalities — here, people over 40, the postpartum period, and trans/gender-diverse people. The same methods apply to everyone, but each group shifts the risk–benefit balance in a specific, examinable way.

The core concept: for over-40s, declining (but non-zero) fertility meets rising VTE/cardiovascular risk — so the questions become which method is safest now and when can contraception finally stop. For postpartum, the drivers are the return of fertility from day 21 and a transient prothrombotic state that restricts oestrogen early. For trans/gender-diverse people, the central message is that gender-affirming hormones are NOT contraception and pregnancy remains possible. Everything is governed by UKMEC (categories 1–4) and FSRH guidance.
UKMEC recap: 1 = no restriction; 2 = benefits generally outweigh risks; 3 = risks generally outweigh benefits (use only if better options unacceptable/unavailable); 4 = unacceptable health risk (do not use).
The Decisive Fork — Which Special-Group Question Is Being Asked?
GroupThe key clinical question
Over 40Which method is safest given age/VTE/cardiovascular risk — and when can contraception stop?
PostpartumWhen does contraception restart (day 21), and is oestrogen safe yet (VTE + breastfeeding)?
Trans/gender-diversePregnancy is still possible — gender-affirming hormones are NOT contraceptive; which method fits their goals + anatomy?
Part A — Over-40s: Principles
  • Fertility declines with age but is not zero — contraception is still needed until the criteria to stop are met
  • Age itself raises VTE, cardiovascular disease and stroke risk → the safety of oestrogen-containing methods falls with age (though age alone is only UKMEC 2 for combined hormonal contraception up to 50)
  • Non-contraceptive benefits become useful — cycle/bleeding control (perimenopausal menorrhagia), the LNG-IUS as the progestogen arm of HRT, and symptom/bone benefits
Part A — Method-by-Method (Over-40)
Combined hormonal contraception (CHC)
  • Can be used to age 50 if no other risk factors (UKMEC 2 for age ≥40); stop at 50 and switch to a safer method
  • First-line preparations over 40: ≤30 µg ethinylestradiol with a levonorgestrel- or norethisterone-containing progestogen (lower VTE/cardiovascular/stroke risk)
  • Non-contraceptive benefits: maintains bone density, reduces vasomotor symptoms and bleeding
Progestogen-only & intrauterine methods
  • Progestogen-only pill (POP) / implant: safe, no age restriction; can continue to 55
  • LNG-IUS (e.g. Mirena): excellent over-40 choice — contraception + menorrhagia treatment + can be the progestogen component of HRT. If inserted at ≥45 for contraception, can stay until 55 (but must be changed at 5 years if used as the HRT progestogen arm)
  • Copper IUD: if inserted at ≥40, can remain until menopause/contraception no longer needed
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA / Depo)
  • Review over-40s regularly
  • At 50, counsel on risks/benefits and switch to an alternative
  • Concern with prolonged use: bone mineral density loss and cardiovascular risk
Part A — When Can Contraception Be Stopped?
📷 Image placeholder — Stopping-contraception flowchart by method — non-hormonal (1 yr amenorrhoea if ≥50, 2 yr if <50), progestogen-only (to 55 or FSH ≥50 → stop 1 yr later), CHC (stop at 50), everyone stops at 55.
The simple rule: everyone can stop contraception at age 55 — spontaneous conception above 55 is exceptionally rare, even with ongoing bleeding.

Before 55, by method + amenorrhoea:

SituationWhen to stop
Non-hormonal method (e.g. copper IUD)After 1 year of amenorrhoea if ≥50, or 2 years if <50
Progestogen-only method (POP/implant/IUS)Continue to 55, or check FSH (see below)
Combined hormonal contraceptionStop at 50 and switch to a progestogen-only/non-hormonal method, then apply the above
The FSH option: in someone ≥50 on a progestogen-only method, a one-off FSH can be used — if in the menopausal range, stop contraception 1 year later. FSH cannot be interpreted on combined hormonal contraception (it suppresses FSH — stop it for 6 weeks first).
HRT is NOT contraception — a person on HRT still needs contraception until 55. The LNG-IUS can serve as both the HRT progestogen and contraception.
Part B — Postpartum: Principles & Timing
  • Contraception is needed from day 21 postpartum — fertility can return by then; before day 21 no contraception is needed
  • If any method other than the POP is started after day 21, use additional precautions for 7 days; a POP started after day 21 needs 2 days of extra precautions
  • After miscarriage/abortion/ectopic: contraception is needed from day 5; methods can usually be started immediately
Lactational amenorrhoea method
  • ~98% effective — but only if all three criteria are met: fully/exclusively breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + under 6 months postpartum
  • If any criterion fails (supplementing feeds, periods return, or over 6 months) → efficacy falls → use another method
Part B — Method-Specific Timing (Postpartum)
📷 Image placeholder — CHC postpartum UKMEC grid — days 0–21 / 3–6 wk / >6 wk against breastfeeding vs not and ± VTE risk factors (the 3-vs-4 distinction), plus the IUD/IUS ≤48h-or-≥4wk rule.
MethodTiming / UKMEC
Progestogen-only (POP, implant, DMPA)Safe from birth (UKMEC 1) — including in breastfeeding; can start immediately postpartum
Combined hormonal contraceptionAvoid early — UKMEC 3 before day 21 if non-breastfeeding with no other VTE risk (UKMEC 4 if breastfeeding or additional VTE risk factors) (peak VTE risk); not breastfeeding + no VTE risk factors → from day 21 (UKMEC 2); breastfeeding → from 6 weeks (UKMEC 2); oestrogen may reduce milk supply
IUD / IUSInsert within 48 hours of delivery, or wait until ≥4 weeks; the 48h–4wk window is UKMEC 3 (↑ expulsion + perforation risk)
Two rules that get examined: (1) pregnancy is prothrombotic and this resolves by ~3 weeks → combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 3 before day 21 if non-breastfeeding with no other VTE risk (UKMEC 4 if breastfeeding or additional VTE risk factors) (defer to 6 weeks if breastfeeding). (2) IUD/IUS: ≤48 hours or ≥4 weeks — avoid the window between (breastfeeding + recent delivery raise perforation risk ~6-fold).
Part C — Trans & Gender-Diverse People
The single most important point: gender-affirming hormones are NOT contraception
  • Testosterone (trans men / people assigned female at birth): often causes amenorrhoea but does NOT prevent pregnancy, and is teratogenic (virilises an XX fetus) → effective contraception is needed if there is a uterus/ovaries and a risk of pregnancy
  • Oestradiol (trans women / people assigned male at birth): impairs spermatogenesis but does NOT reliably prevent pregnancy → someone not surgically sterilised having vaginal sex where pregnancy is possible must still use contraception
  • GnRH analogues used to suppress gonadal function cannot be relied on for contraception
  • The rule: assess anatomy + activity, not gender identity. Anyone with a uterus/ovaries (or producing sperm) having sex that could cause pregnancy needs contraception
Method considerations
  • People assigned female at birth on testosterone: progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, IUS) and the copper IUD contain no oestrogen → preferred (don’t oppose masculinisation); progestogens + testosterone-induced amenorrhoea can also help menstrual suppression/dysphoria
  • Oestrogen-containing (CHC): no absolute contraindication from testosterone itself, but many prefer to avoid oestrogen (opposes masculinisation; theoretical VTE concern)
  • Testosterone should be continued — add contraception alongside, don’t stop gender-affirming therapy
  • People assigned male at birth on oestrogen: if fertile sperm may persist (no vasectomy/orchidectomy) and having vaginal sex with pregnancy risk → barrier/partner or other contraception
Counselling
  • Inclusive, affirming, individualised
  • Discuss fertility + fertility preservation
  • STI protection (condoms — including for anal/other sex)
  • Cervical screening if a cervix is present
  • Be mindful that examinations/menstruation may cause dysphoria
Exam Pearls
UKMEC 1–4
1 = no restriction, 2 = benefits > risks, 3 = risks > benefits (avoid if alternatives), 4 = do not use.
Over-40s
Fertility low but not zero; CHC to 50 (≤30µg ethinylestradiol + levonorgestrel/norethisterone; UKMEC 2); POP/implant/IUS no age limit; DMPA — review, switch at 50 (bone/cardiovascular); LNG-IUS = contraception + menorrhagia + HRT progestogen.
Stopping
Everyone can stop at 55; non-hormonal → 1yr amenorrhoea if ≥50 (2yr if <50); FSH option ≥50 on progestogen-only (stop 1yr later; can’t interpret on CHC); HRT is NOT contraception.
Postpartum
Contraception from day 21 (extra precautions 7 days, or 2 days for POP); POP/implant/DMPA safe from birth; CHC — UKMEC 3 before day 21 if non-breastfeeding with no other VTE risk (UKMEC 4 if breastfeeding or additional VTE risk factors), from day 21 if not breastfeeding, from 6 weeks if breastfeeding; IUD/IUS ≤48h or ≥4 weeks.
Lactational amenorrhoea
~98% effective only if fully breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + under 6 months.
Trans/gender-diverse
Gender-affirming hormones (testosterone, oestradiol, GnRH analogues) are NOT contraception; testosterone is teratogenic; progestogen-only + copper IUD preferred on testosterone; assess anatomy + activity, not identity; inclusive counselling, fertility, STI/cervical screening.
